directing-1: I came to directing through the stage, as actor, playwright and manager, so I will tell you what I look for first: the order of the work. Before the first rehearsal there is reading, choosing, planning and listening to designers, and each stage has its own question. As you read this lesson, write down the four lines of the director's job in your own words and put a date beside each one for your own scene. A director who cannot say what the work is for each week will find the weeks do the choosing for them. Notice where the screen version differs, because the same habit takes a different form there.

Read the play before you decide anything about it, and read it more than once. On the first read you will get pictures in your head; keep them, but do not trust them yet. The French scene, cut at each entrance or exit, is a practical tool for finding what each character wants in a stretch of action. When you divide your scene, say aloud what changes at each division, and if nothing changes, you have cut in the wrong place. I would also have you time the reading, because a scene has a pace that only shows when it is spoken, and the pace is part of the story shape.

A theme is a short statement you can act on, not a message you push on the audience. Ask the play questions and let the answers settle, and then ask who is in the room. This lesson wants a one-line theme and a sentence about the audience, and I would have you write both before you plan a single move. Check the theme against your scene: does every beat serve it, or only some? Cut the beat that does not, as I cut only what I could justify. If the theme comes out as a slogan, it is too loud, and the audience will disengage.

On screen nothing in the picture is accidental, so the look must come from the idea. Mise-en-scène is the overall look built from setting, character, lighting and composition, and it answers the same question I put to a stage setting: does it help the words or compete with them? Take your theme and write three things that must be in the frame and three that must not. This is the screen version of removing what the audience looks at instead of listening to. Keep the list short and test it against the scene before you commit to a design.
directing-2: I taught by setting a small problem and talking it through, and this lesson is two such problems. The given circumstances are the world the actor answers in: who, where, when, and the facts of the play. The 'if' is the question that sets the imagination moving, and it works because it admits that it is only a supposition. Write the circumstances for your scene in one breath, and then write one honest 'if' that does not tell anyone what to feel. Watch for the point where the source differs on what is meant by 'the Method', and keep to the exercises as the book gives them.

A play is too big to swallow whole, so we carve it into units and give each an objective. The objective must be a verb, because a noun makes the actor show an idea instead of doing something. Try this on your own scene: name the units, give each a verb phrase, and test it by saying 'I want to...' aloud. Keep the units few; a dozen small ones will scatter the actor's attention. Then use the tests from the book for a right objective, such as whether it is aimed at the partner, and cut any objective that fails one.

The camera is far more intimate than the old stage, and acting that fills the back row looks false at close range. What the actor does with a thought can be seen in the eyes, so ask for less, not more. In this lesson look at what a director asks for on screen and compare it with the stage version of the same objective. Try the same unit twice, once for a room of forty and once for a lens, and note what you took away. The want stays the same; the size of the action changes. Do not ask for a copy of an earlier take, but re-set the circumstances.
directing-3: No one acts alone. I asked a student whom he was in communion with at that moment, and he said nobody; I told him that we are always in some contact, even with ourselves. Communion is the give and take between two actors, and adaptation is how each adjusts to the other. In your rehearsal, give the actors something to do to each other, not a feeling to show. Watch whether each adjusts to what the partner does. If they stop adapting, they are playing at the audience, and you will see it at once.

Small objectives matter only if they lead somewhere. The through-line of action is the path through the play, and the super-objective is the aim that gathers every unit toward it. Any detail that does not serve it will stand out as wrong. Name your super-objective as a verb, and try three names, as the book does with Woe from Wit, to see which one explains the most. Then name the counteraction, the force that pulls the other way, because a line without resistance goes nowhere. Check every unit against the line you chose.

A rehearsal week is made of small things: a note, a breath, a pause that lets thought arrive. Give notes you can act on, one at a time, in terms of what to do and not what to feel. Plan the week in landmarks, so that each day has a purpose and the actors know what is wanted of them. Keep the room safe and warm, and stop when someone is distressed. When you try the day-backwards exercise, give it ten minutes, and ask for short, physical answers.

A film set has a thousand moving parts, and the actor must keep the performance true from the start of a take to the end while the editor shapes it afterwards. Your job is to hold the shape of the whole so that the actor can attend to the next moment. Rehearse the unit for the camera, and agree what the actor will do before the take. Remember that the line you built backwards from the scene still runs under every shot, even when the scenes are shot out of order. Keep a note of what each actor needs to remember.
directing-4: Training the stage begins silent, because most storytelling is not words. I put the actor's body first. Learn the parts of the stage and the order in which they draw the eye, and then learn when a posture overrides them. Try this: stand on the stage with nothing to say, and move so that the audience looks where you want. Notice what your body does when you decide to reveal or hide something. The body can find a choice that thought misses, and this lesson is a way to look for it.

The stage picture is made of distance, level and crossing. Three actors in a line make a flat picture, and one stepping forward makes a triangle with a point of focus. Distance tells the audience about the relationship before anyone speaks. Draw your scene as a series of pictures, mark where the power sits, and ask whether each change serves the story. Build a small database of images you like, and note what each does. When a picture works, find out why before you copy it.

A frame is a picture the director chooses, and the audience cannot look outside it. Composition arranges people, objects and setting inside it, to balance or unbalance, reveal or hide. Keep the line of screen direction clear, and decide before you shoot who is on which side. Take your stage blocking and redraw it for a camera: what must be in the frame, and what can be implied? Do not teach risky movement to an actor without a qualified teacher, and keep the capstone free of falls and lifts.
directing-5: A shot is a decision about what the audience sees and how it feels. A close-up creates intimacy, and an extreme long shot suggests distance. Choose the size, the lens and the movement for a moment, and say why each choice is motivated. If you cannot say why, change it. I would have you cut the same four shots by length first, then by movement, then by tone, as the methods in the lesson describe, and write what each cut made the viewer feel. I wrote about the clash of images, but you will learn it by cutting.

Continuity is the art of not being noticed. The master shot gives the whole scene, coverage gives the details, and the line keeps the viewer oriented in space. Draw the line for your scene before you set the camera, and cross it only on purpose. Parallel editing lets two actions run together, and you can use it to raise tension. When you plan coverage, list the shots you need, and then check that each one will cut together without confusion.

Kuleshov showed that the audience reads meaning from the order of shots, so the same face can look different beside soup, a child in a coffin or a woman. I took that further and called montage a collision: an idea arises from two independent shots meeting. Try it with two shots of your own and ask what idea appears that is in neither. Discontinuity on purpose can break the smooth flow, but only if you know the rule you are breaking. Keep a log of your cuts and what each did.

A stage has no cut, but it has transitions: lighting changes, set moves, an actor crossing the dark. A transition is the way the audience moves from one scene to another, and it can keep the tension or let it drop. Treat it as an edit: decide where each scene should end and what should carry over. Loops can repeat an image like a refrain. Watch for where to stop, because a transition that goes on too long loses the thread you built.
directing-6: Fix the performance space early, because designs, ground plan and blocking all depend on it. I started from an empty space and a watching audience, and I would have you start there too. Compare proscenium, thrust and round: how the audience sits changes what they see and how close they feel. Draw a ground plan for each, and put one entrance and one exit on each. If you can stage in all three, you can stage anywhere. For a film, ask whether a location or a soundstage serves the story better.

Designers are collaborators and equal voices, not people who decorate your idea. Before each meeting read the play, list what that designer needs, bring pictures, and say the budget aloud. A budget is a story too: every line says what the production values. Apply the stripping test: add back one element at a time, and keep only what you can justify. When you brief a designer, give the one idea the production serves, as the 1970 Dream did with its white box and its doubled roles.

Tech is where the design joins the actors, and you have little time to do what took weeks in rehearsal. Be a steady presence, tell the actors what to expect, and protect their attention. After the opening, review the work honestly and write down what you would keep and what you would change. On screen, the handover is similar: the picture goes to the editor. Keep your notes short and specific, and give credit where it is due. A review that names only problems teaches less than one that also names what to keep.
directing-cap: Choose a short scene of two or three characters, about three minutes, from a public-domain play or your own writing. You will direct it twice, once for the stage and once for the screen. Write the French scenes, the objectives as verbs, the super-objective, a ground plan and a shot list before you rehearse. Check each objective against the tests: is it aimed at the partner, is it active, is it clear? The plan will change in rehearsal, but you will know why.

Use the rehearsal order in miniature: a read-through, script work on each French scene, blocking, a stumble-through, scene work and a run. Warm up the group first. Keep your notes in terms of what to do, not what to feel. Shoot only what you rehearsed, and record both versions. Do not ask for a copy of an earlier success; re-set the circumstances each time. Keep the work safe, and stop if anyone is distressed.

Show both versions to a small audience and ask what they believed. Use the question 'I do not believe you' as a test, not a verdict. Score each version against the rubric, mark the moments that did not ring true, and group them by unit. Write one fix for each group, and choose one thing to keep. Then rehearse the fixes and record again. A review that leads to a better next run is worth more than a grade.
